UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

    Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company            )

                    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                   SOUTHERN INDIANA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company

d/b/a CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (“SIGE” or “Company”) submits this Motion for Leave

to Answer and Answer to address certain comments and protests filed in response to SIGE’s

January 6, 2026 complaint in this proceeding.2           In the Complaint, SIGE requests that the

Commission direct the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) to revise its

Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to include a

cost recovery schedule, which the Company has proposed for recovery of costs associated with an

emergency order issued by the U.S. Secretary of Energy (“Secretary”) on December 23, 2025

(“DOE Order”) pursuant to section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and section 301(b)

of the Department of Energy Organization Act.3 The DOE Order states that the Secretary has

determined an emergency exists within the MISO region—specifically, in the northern and central

zones of MISO—and directs the Company to ensure that Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley Generating

“rate recovery is available” and directing the Company to “file with the [Commission] tariff

revisions or waivers necessary to effectuate the Order.”7 SIGE has requested a narrow form of

relief that MISO does not oppose. Specifically, MISO has stated that it “does not oppose the

addition of a cost recovery schedule that would permit SIGE to recover the costs incurred as a

result of its efforts to comply with the DOE Order.”8 In addition, MISO states it “supports the

addition of a cost recovery schedule to the Tariff” and believes the Commission’s acceptance of

SIGE’s proposed cost recovery mechanism “would further compliance with the DOE Order by

both SIGE and MISO.”9

Culley Unit 2 and Culley Unit 3, with a combined name plate capacity of 368.9 MW. Culley Unit 2 is the
focus of the recent DOE Order, and is owned and operated by CenterPoint Energy, Inc.’s operating

          Two entities filed protests urging the Commission to reject or deny the Complaint,10 and

other intervenors requested that the Commission either set the Complaint for hearing or, in the

alternative, require a MISO stakeholder process to address cost causation and benefit issues.11 One

joint intervention takes no position on SIGE’s requested relief but requests that none of the Order

Costs be allocated to the MISO South Region.12 SIGE respectfully submits that the protests and

comments opposing the Complaint lack merit and should be rejected.

I.       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

         The material facts and legal issues presented in SIGE’s Complaint are on “all fours” with

those presented in Consumers Energy’s complaint in Docket No. EL25-90-000. SIGE respectfully

submits that, based on the Commission’s order granting the Consumers Energy complaint,13 the

relief requested by SIGE in this case should also be granted.

4 (filed Jan. 26, 2026) (Michigan AG Protest); Protest of the Sierra Club, et al., Docket No. EL26-38-000,
at 2 (filed Jan. 26, 2026) (PIOs Comments).

Commission, Docket No. EL26-38-000, at 11 (filed Jan. 23, 2026) (ICC Comments). SIGE notes that the
ICC Comments specifically ask the Commission to deny SIGE’s request for a cost-recovery mechanism “at
this time” and instead require SIGE to provide further cost and benefit information, and direct the parties
to conduct a stakeholder process to vet the appropriate mechanism for cost recovery under 202(c) of the
FPA. ICC Comments at 3. As explained further in Sections III.B and III.D, these arguments should be
rejected.

         First, challenges to the lawfulness and validity of the DOE Order are outside the scope of

this proceeding, as the Commission found in Consumers Energy.14 Any arguments lodged in this

FERC proceeding that challenge the validity of the DOE Order or its findings are impermissible

collateral attacks that should be rejected.15

        Second, SIGE has a constitutional and a statutory right to recover costs associated with the

DOE Order, and there is no basis for deferring adoption of the proposed cost recovery schedule at

this time. The new MISO cost recovery schedule that SIGE has proposed provides that, to the

extent that the Company’s costs associated with the DOE Order are not covered by market

revenue,16 such costs will be allocated on a load-share ratio basis to Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”)

in MISO’s northern and central zones—which are the zones DOE specifically identified in

declaring the emergency to be served by the continued operation of Culley Unit 2. This is the

same mechanism that the Commission found to be just and reasonable in the Consumers Energy

complaint proceeding. The Commission should reject arguments that SIGE must identify who

benefits from the continued operation of Culley Unit 2 before the Commission can direct that the

proposed cost recovery schedule be added to the MISO Tariff because such arguments

specifically in the northern and central zones, and that it is necessary for Culley Unit 2 to remain

connection with the DOE Order and that the Company is entitled to recover such costs (net of any

        Fourth, the Commission should also reject calls for a MISO stakeholder process before the

or direct MISO to commence a stakeholder process, and (iii) swiftly issue an order directing MISO

to make a compliance filing to adopt add the proposed cost recovery schedule.

 II.     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

        The Commission has discretion to accept answers to protests and regularly does so when

the information provided in the proposed answer will assist the Commission in its decision-making

process.24 Good cause exists for the Commission to accept this answer because it corrects certain

misstatements in various comments filed in response to the Complaint, will “clarify the issues in

dispute,” will help the Commission “achieve a more complete and accurate record” in this

proceeding,25 and will further assist the Commission in its decision-making process. Acceptance

of this answer will not impede or delay Commission action.26 SIGE respectfully requests that the

Commission accept this answer and consider the points raised herein.27

III.    ANSWER

        A.      The Commission Should Decline to Address Collateral Attacks on the Validity of
                the DOE Order or Its Determinations

        This proceeding is not the proper forum for challenging the DOE Order’s determination of

an energy emergency or its direction that SIGE ensure that Culley Unit 2 remains available to

operate during the term of the DOE Order. In its protest, for example, the Michigan Attorney

        There is also no reason for the Commission to delay granting the relief requested in the

Complaint until the “legal validity”33 of the DOE Order has been fully litigated. Requiring MISO

to revise its Tariff to add the proposed cost recovery schedule will not bar challenges to specific

costs that SIGE may seek to recover in the future. However, amending the MISO Tariff to include

an appropriate cost recovery schedule is appropriate in light of potential future challenges based

filed rate doctrine does not apply to the recovery of costs under FPA section 202(c).34

        There have been no judicial decrees pausing or in any way limiting the DOE Order’s

implementation of a cost-recovery mechanism that protects SIGE’s constitutional and statutory

rights to recover costs associated with the DOE Order (net of market revenue). Thus, to protect

SIGE’s right to recover the costs currently being incurred, the Commission should order MISO to

amend its Tariff to include the proposed cost recovery mechanism without delay.

         B.       Commission Approval of the Proposed Cost Recovery Schedule Does Not Require
                 SIGE to Establish Cost Causation or Benefits

        Certain intervenors argue that the Commission should require a hearing to examine

whether the relief requested in the Complaint would impose cost increases on ratepayers without

commensurate benefits.36 These comments reflect a fundamental misunderstanding of FPA

section 202(c) of the FPA’s legal framework and purpose.

        As SIGE explained in its Complaint, FPA sections 205 and 206 are inapplicable when a

generator is required to operate pursuant to section 202(c) and seeks to recover costs incurred to

do so. Instead, as the Commission held in Consumers Energy, it is just and reasonable to allocate

such costs based on the scope and nature of the emergency declared in the relevant 202(c) order.37

Here, the Secretary of Energy has declared an emergency based on resource adequacy concerns in

specific zones within the MISO region.              As SIGE explained in its Complaint and as the

Commission found in Consumers Energy, based on the DOE Order’s express references to MISO’s

northern and central zones,38 the scope of the emergency includes MISO Zones 1 through 7.39

          C.      A Commission Hearing Is Not Warranted Because There Are No Material Facts
                 in Dispute

         The Commission has discretion regarding whether to order an evidentiary hearing.44

Typically, the Commission only orders a hearing when doing so is required to resolve disputed

issues of fact.45 “No evidentiary hearing is required if FERC can adequately resolve the disputed

issues on the written record.”46 Moreover, it is well established that “mere allegations of disputed

facts are insufficient to mandate a hearing.”47

         Several commenters and protestors assert that the Commission should decline to act on the

Complaint until after the Commission has conducted a hearing.48 The Commission should reject

that position. The Complaint seeks an order requiring MISO to adopt the cost recovery schedule

SIGE has proposed to ensure that the Company may recover costs associated with the DOE Order,

net of market revenue—understanding that any actual costs the Company seeks to recover will be

addressed in a future cost recovery proceeding before the Commission.49 There are no disputed

facts that require resolution before this relief can be granted. Rather, it is undisputed that:

        The DOE Order requires SIGE to take actions to ensure Culley Unit 2’s continued
         availability (among other things).

        SIGE is already incurring and will continue to incur costs to comply with the DOE Order.

         D.      A MISO Stakeholder Process Is Unwarranted

        A MISO stakeholder process would be equally unproductive and inadvisable.

        First, in the Consumers Energy complaint proceeding, Consumers Energy requested the

exact same relief that SIGE is requesting in this proceeding – namely, a requirement for MISO to

adopt a cost recovery mechanism in its Tariff to allow for recovery of costs associated with a

202(c) order. When intervenors in the Consumers Energy complaint proceeding called for a MISO

stakeholder process, the Commission held that it was “not necessary”53 because interested parties

had an opportunity to comment on the complaint proceeding.54

        Second, a MISO stakeholder process raises the same concerns of delaying cost recovery as

FERC hearing procedures.

        Third, FPA section 202(c) contemplates that the Commission—not MISO—will address

the cost recovery issues arising from the DOE Order. In this Complaint proceeding, interested

stakeholders have had the opportunity to opine on the Company’s proposed cost recovery schedule
